result.summary: Hesiod continues the genealogy of the Titans and their offspring: the children of Ceto and Phorcys, the rivers and Oceanids born of Tethys and Ocean, the children of Theia, Eurybia, Eos and Styx. The section ends with a long praise of Hecate, daughter of Phoebe and Coeus, honoured above all by Zeus.

scenes.title: Offspring of Ceto and Phorcys
scenes.summary: Ceto and Phorcys have their youngest child, the snake guarding the golden apples.

place.name: the secret places of the dark earth at its great bounds

scenes.title: Rivers and Oceanids
scenes.summary: Tethys bears to Ocean the many rivers and the three thousand daughters, including Styx.

place.name: the earth and the deep waters

scenes.title: Sun, Moon, Dawn and Winds
scenes.summary: Theia, Eurybia and Eos bear the heavenly lights, the winds and the stars.

scenes.title: Styx and her children
scenes.summary: Styx bears Zelus, Nike, Cratos and Bia. She joins Zeus first against the Titans and is made the oath of the gods.
scenes.stakes: Zeus's war against the Titans; Styx and her children gain lasting honour by siding with him.

scenes.title: Hecate and her honours
scenes.summary: Phoebe and Coeus have Leto, Asteria and Hecate. Zeus honours Hecate, who aids kings, warriors, athletes, sailors and herdsmen, and nurses the young.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Zeus as wielder of lightning.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains why the gods swear their greatest oath by Styx.
Shows Hecate's cult importance, invoked in every sacrifice.

analysis.text: The genealogies order the cosmos, tracing natural forces such as rivers, winds and stars to divine parents. Zeus rewards loyalty, establishing the justice of his rule.
The long praise of Hecate is unusual and suggests Hesiod's local devotion or her importance in Boeotian cult. The river catalogue reflects Greek geographic knowledge from Asia Minor to Italy.

legacy.text: Swearing by the River Styx became a lasting literary figure for an unbreakable oath, appearing in Virgil and Dante.
Hecate later became associated with witchcraft and magic in Greek and Roman writers.

fun_facts.text: The numbers in brackets inside the text, such as 1615, are footnote markers from the translation, not part of Hesiod's poem.

language_notes.text: "Bare" is the archaic past tense of "bear": gave birth to. "Awful" here means inspiring awe or dread, not merely bad.
"Have youths in their keeping" means they watch over and nurture young men as they grow up.
"Neat-ankled" is a fixed epithet for graceful, slender-ankled goddesses; the sense is "trim-ankled".
"Severally dwell" means each local people knows the name of the river beside which it lives.
"A goddess mating in love with a god" stresses that this union is of two deities, unlike the later winds said to be born differently.
"Wherein God leads them" refers to Zeus; the translator uses a singular "God" for the ruler of the gods.
The Titans were the older generation of gods. Zeus called the gods to Olympus before the war against them, the Titanomachy.
"Olympian Lightener" is Zeus, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
"Bare" is the archaic past tense of "bear", meaning gave birth to.
"Unfruitful sea" translates a standard Greek description of the sea as barren, in contrast with farmland.
"Earth-Shaker" is a title of Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes, whom sailors prayed to.
"Kine" is an archaic plural of cow, meaning cattle.
"1617" is a stray footnote number from the edition, not part of the poem.
"Saw the light of all-seeing Dawn" means were born and grew up; Hecate protects children from birth onward.

context_notes.text: The golden apples belong to the Hesperides, at the western edge of the world. The snake is the dragon Ladon, who guards them.
The list names real rivers, such as the Nile and Scamander in Troy's plain, spanning Egypt, Greece and Asia Minor.
Helius, Selene and Eos are the Sun, Moon and Dawn, children of the Titans Hyperion and Theia.
The gods swore their most binding oaths by the waters of the river Styx, as this line explains.
Leto became the mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.
Hecate is a goddess associated with boundaries, help and later magic; Hesiod stresses her wide, benevolent powers.
The Titans were the older generation of gods, overthrown by Zeus; Hecate unusually keeps her old privileges under the new rule.
Kings gave judgements in assemblies; Hesiod elsewhere values just kings, so Hecate's favour is significant.

literary_notes.text: The long list of rivers is a traditional epic catalogue, giving a sense of vast scope and showing the poet's command of knowledge.
Fixed descriptive phrases like "neat-ankled" and "glorious among goddesses" are characteristic epic epithets.
The poet admits human limits: mortals cannot name every river, which sets the narrator's knowledge beside that of the Muses.
Power, Force, Victory and Emulation live permanently with Zeus, which shows his rule as backed by constant strength and success.
The short closing line sets Zeus's absolute rule against the long account of his supporters, ending the passage with emphatic simplicity.
"Dark-gowned" and the repeated "mild" characterize Leto by her gentle nature and her traditional descriptive tag.
Hecate is portrayed as a generous giver of wealth, answering prayers according to her will.
"Easily" is repeated for giving and taking away, showing her effortless, sovereign power.
The closing "from the beginning" and "nurse of the young" return to earlier statements, rounding off the praise of Hecate.
